p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: The first year after your course is when good habits form, and when a lot of people quietly stop diving. These tips help you keep going and keep it fun.

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Skills fade fast. Try to get a few easy dives in within a couple of months of your course, ideally with the shop where you trained. Fun dives, club trips and local quarry days all count. If it's been a while, take a refresher. Many shops suggest one if you haven't dived in about six months and have fewer than 20 dives. PADI calls theirs ReActivate ; other agencies have their own.

t: Make your first trip an easy one
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Pick warm, calm, clear water with short boat rides. A group trip with your own dive shop is a great first choice. Tell the dive operator you're newly certified. They'll pair you well and pick suitable sites. Bring your certification card (or app) and your logbook. Operators may ask how many dives you have and when your last one was. See our trip reports for places other divers recommend.

t: Buy gear in the right order
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: You don't need to buy everything at once. A common order: Mask, snorkel, fins and boots. Fit matters most here, and they're the cheapest to own. A dive computer. It goes everywhere with you, keeps your log and is the gear most divers buy next. See Technology Explained . An exposure suit that fits you, if you dive often in the same conditions. BCD and regulator last, once you know what kind of diving you'll do. Rent them until then, and have your own serviced on schedule once you buy.

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Your logbook is your proof of experience for trips and courses, and a record you'll enjoy later. Write down the site, your buddy, conditions, weight and what you saw. The DiveFolk Logbook keeps your dive computer data and paper notes together in one file you own.

t: Stay safe between dives and flights
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Flying after diving. DAN recommends waiting at least 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive and at least 18 hours after several dives a day or several days of diving. Have a plan for emergencies. DAN membership includes a 24/7 emergency hotline and travel assistance. Dive accident insurance is a separate plan; check what you're covered for before you travel. Know your limits. Stay within your training and your computer's limits, and call a dive if something doesn't feel right. Anyone can call any dive.

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Most divers take an advanced course next, which adds a deeper dive, navigation and a few specialties you choose. Practicing buoyancy on every dive pays off more than any gadget. And use AI to help you prepare: our DiveFolk AI prompts help you plan trips, check gear and review skills. t: Does your dive computer split one dive into two?
p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: How to stop it on Shearwater, Garmin, Suunto and Apple Watch, and how to merge dives that are already split. You pop up for a minute to fix a mask, help a buddy clear their ears or check where the boat is, then go back down. Later, your log shows two dives instead of one. Your dive count is off, and neither piece shows the real dive.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Every dive computer decides a dive is over after you've been at the surface for a set time. If that time is short, a quick trip up ends the dive, and going back down starts a new one. Many computers let you make that time longer.

t: How to stop it, by brand
p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Look for End Dive Delay in the computer's settings. Shearwater support told us the default is 1 minute and recommends 10 minutes if your dives are getting split. Shearwater Cloud can't merge dives that are already split; Shearwater says it is looking at adding merging to its Dive Shearwater app. Source: Shearwater support, October 2026.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Garmin's Descent manuals list End Dive Delay under Dive Setup (hold MENU, then Dive Setup). It sets how long the watch waits after you surface before it ends and saves the dive. Choose a longer delay. We haven't found a way to merge split dives in Garmin Connect. Source: Descent Mk3 owner's manual, Dive Setup .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Use Dive end time in Dive settings (scroll down from the pre-dive or surface screen). The default is 5 minutes and you can set 1 to 10. If you go back down before the time runs out, it's the same dive. Source: Suunto Ocean and Suunto Nautic dive settings.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: When you come up shallower than about 5 meters, Oceanic+ asks whether you're finished and starts a 3-minute countdown. If you aren't done, start descending again and it returns to dive mode. Source: Oceanic+ FAQ .

t: Mares, Scubapro, Aqualung, Oceanic, Cressi and others
p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: We're still checking these brands' official manuals before we publish exact steps. In the meantime, look in your manual for a setting called "dive end time," "end dive delay" or "end of dive." If you've found it on your computer, tell us and we'll add it here.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: The DiveFolk Logbook joins them for you, for any brand. It suggests which pieces belong together using the time at the surface and, when your computer records it, your tank pressure. You can undo any join, then download a clean log. The free desktop program Subsurface can also merge selected dives. Settings checked November 1, 2026. Menus change with firmware updates, so check your own manual too. More guides in Technology Explained

t: Your dive tech, in plain words
x: Short guides to the technology divers use every day. They explain how things work; your training, your dive computer's manual and your instructor come first.

Your dive computer tracks your depth and time and uses a decompression model to estimate how much nitrogen your body has taken on. From that, it shows a few numbers that matter most: No-decompression limit (NDL). How many more minutes you can stay at your current depth and still ascend directly to the surface, with a safety stop. Ascent rate. Most computers warn you if you come up too fast. Slow ascents are one of the simplest safety habits. Safety stop. Many computers count down a stop near 15 feet at the end of a dive. Gas. If you dive nitrox, your computer needs the right oxygen percentage

t: Does your dive computer split one dive into two?
x: A quick trip to the surface can make your computer log one dive as two. Our guide explains why, shows the setting to change on Shearwater, Garmin, Suunto and Apple Watch, and how to fix dives that are already split. Read the split dives guide

Many computers, including Shearwater and Garmin dive computers, use a decompression model called Bühlmann. Gradient factors are two percentages that make that model more or less conservative. GF high sets how close to the model's limit you can be when you reach the surface. For most recreational diving, this is the number that matters most. A lower GF high means shorter no-deco times and more margin. GF low mainly shapes deeper stops on dives that need decompression, so it rarely affects typical recreational dives. Settings like "low, medium, high" conservatism are usually preset gradient fact

With air integration, a small transmitter screws into your regulator's first stage and sends your tank pressure wirelessly to your dive computer. The computer can then show your pressure, your gas use and an estimate of time remaining. The transmitter has to be paired with your computer and has its own battery. Signals can drop out briefly, especially when another diver's transmitter is close by. Many divers also keep an analog pressure gauge as a backup.

Dive computers and apps save your dives in different file types. Knowing which one you have makes it easier to move your log where you want it. Format What it is Where you'll see it UDDF Universal Dive Data Format: an open format that many dive log programs can read and write. Exports from Shearwater Cloud and other apps. The DiveFolk Logbook reads it. DL7 The dive log format from DAN (Divers Alert Network). Files end in .zxu. Some dive apps export and import it. CSV A plain spreadsheet file: rows and columns of text. Opens in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers and almost anything else. FIT Garmin'

A dive log is hard to rebuild if you lose it. A simple routine keeps it safe: After each trip, export your dives from your dive computer's app (UDDF and CSV are good choices). Keep everything in one folder you own: your spreadsheet, the computer files and photos of your paper logbook pages. Keep a second copy somewhere else, such as a cloud drive or an external drive. An app that syncs to the cloud is convenient, but it's not the same as a copy you control. Get the free DiveFolk dive log spreadsheet

t: Are your dive times off by an hour?
x: Most dive computers keep whatever clock time you set. Fly somewhere in a different time zone without changing it, and every dive on the trip is logged an hour or more off. Your paper log and your computer won't agree, and dives can land on the wrong day. Before a trip: set your computer's clock to local time when you arrive. Watches that sync with your phone may do this for you, but check. After a trip: the DiveFolk Logbook has a Clock fix for each dive, and if you add your paper log it tells you when the times disagree and by how much.

These are the dive tech headaches divers ask about most often in forums. Tell us which one you want first at hello@divefolk.com . t: Thinking about diving? Try it first.
p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: You don't have to sign up for a full course to find out if you like breathing underwater. Here's how to try it, what learning involves, and how to pick a place to learn.

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: Most dive shops offer a short try-dive. PADI calls it Discover Scuba Diving , and other training agencies have their own versions. You learn a few basic skills in water shallow enough to stand up in, then swim around with an instructor right next to you. It's a low-pressure way to find out whether you can clear your ears and whether you feel comfortable underwater. It's for ages 10 and up in the PADI version. It isn't a certification. You can only dive with a professional supervising you. If your try-dive includes an open water dive, the instructor may be able to count it toward a full course

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: Before any scuba program you'll fill in a short diver medical questionnaire . It was written by diving doctors working with DAN and the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society. If you answer "no" to everything, you're set. A "yes" doesn't mean you can't dive; it means a doctor needs to sign off first. Do that before your trip, not at the dock. See the questionnaire (PDF)

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: The first full certification is usually called Open Water Diver . In the PADI version it has three parts: Knowledge: reading or online lessons with short quizzes. Many people do this at home before the pool. Pool sessions: practicing skills like clearing your mask and sharing air in calm, shallow water. Four open water dives: in a lake, quarry or the ocean, usually over two days. You'll need to swim 200 meters (or 300 with mask, fins and snorkel) and float for 10 minutes, with no time limit on the swim. Once certified, you can dive with a buddy to about 60 feet (18 meters). Kids from 10 to 14

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: The well-known training agencies, such as PADI, SSI, NAUI, SDI and RAID, are all widely accepted around the world. The instructor and the shop matter more than the logo on the card. Questions worth asking: How many students per instructor in the pool and in open water? Where are the pool sessions and open water dives, and when? What's included in the price: online lessons, gear rental, open water dives, entry fees? Which gear do I need to buy? Most shops ask you to own a mask, snorkel, fins and boots. t: Dominica: easy boat dives, lots of life, and a lot to do on land
x: By Alex, DiveFolk's founder. 14 dives over five days, from a new diver's point of view. The west coast from the dive boat. Where Dominica, Caribbean. Stayed at the Fort Young Hotel in Roseau, which has its own dive shop. When December 7 to 11, 2025 Organized by A group trip run by Aquatic Adventures, a dive shop in Virginia Diving Morning boat dives on the west coast, plus night and training dives from the hotel's dock Conditions Water 79 to 82 °F. Visibility 60 to 100 feet on boat dives. Mostly light current. Most dives 40 to 90 feet. Exposure A 3 mm wetsuit on day one, then just a rash guard

The sites I dove included Champagne Reef, Scotts Head Drop Off, Soufrière Pinnacle, Solomon, Witches Point, Dangleben's Pinnacle and a wall dive. Champagne Reef is the best known: volcanic gas bubbles stream up from the sea floor. Some favorite moments from my log: a turtle in a small canyon between pinnacles on the first dive, parrotfish everywhere at Champagne South, and a pufferfish with blue, glittery eyes. On a night dive off the hotel dock we saw bioluminescence on the way out, and back at the dock, moray eels were cleaning up lionfish scraps. An honest note: most of the coral I saw was

I loved the dives, but I especially loved walking around Roseau and eating where the locals eat, including neighborhoods people told me to avoid. I never had a problem. Use the same common sense you would in any city, and get out of the hotel. Don't skip the side trips. Dominica is mountains and rainforest, and the hikes to waterfalls and river gorges were some of the best days of the trip. Plan them for afternoons or a day off from diving. Trafalgar Falls. Worth a day off from diving. Walking around Roseau. Heading out with the Fort Young crew.

Pack boots and a thin wetsuit or rash guard; the water is warm. Bring a dive light if you want to try a night dive off the dock. Dock dives at Fort Young depend on the cruise ship schedule. When a ship stays late, night dives can't start until it leaves, so plan for some waiting. The dive shop posts the week's sites on a board, so you know what's coming. See our week's board .
